title: Go, Madhava, go
hookLine: Radha waits all night in the place they agreed on, and at dawn he finally turns up
carry: bhakti has room for honest anger at god

cards: The plan was simple: meet in the bower by the river, tonight. Radha goes. She waits.
The moon comes up over the forest, and he doesn't come. She hears a leaf move and thinks it's him. It isn't.
The whole night goes by like that. Then, at dawn, there he is, walking up through the trees with the look of someone who hasn't slept. Before he can say a word, she knows where he's been.
What does a devotee, in a poem about God, say to God at a moment like this? Jayadeva gives her the floor.

teach.b: The poem lingers on what she sees, in paraphrase. His eyes are red from a night without sleep. There are marks on him, traces left by someone else.
And her song has a refrain sharp enough to sting: go, Madhava, go, Keshava. Don't speak your deceiving words. Go to the one who kept you up all night.
She doesn't soften it or pretend to be fine. And the poem doesn't correct her, not yet. It lets her anger stand on the page, in front of the one the poem calls Lord.
Vaishnava poetics has a name for this loving anger: mana, the wounded pride of a lover who knows her worth. It's treated as one of love's real moods, not a fault to hide.
Read, as some devotees read it, with Radha as the soul, the scene suggests that bhakti doesn't have to be polite. A devotee may come before God disappointed, even furious, and the relationship holds.

That's the teaching, plainly: bhakti has room for honest anger at God. Many Hindus who pray know this: you can bring the hurt to the shrine as it is. In the poem it more than holds: Krishna won't stop seeking her.
Later, her friend will gently tell her she's held on long enough. But first, the poem gives her this.

teach.h: THE COMPLAINT KEEPS HER IN THE ROOM.
teach.b: An honest complaint is itself a way of staying in the room.
Indifference would say nothing. Radha says everything.

how: In Vaishnava devotional performance, Radha's mana, her loving anger, is a recognized mood: singers and Odissi or Bharatanatyam dancers perform her song of dismissal at dawn as part of the Gita Govinda's story of separation and reunion.

o: obedience that never questions the beloved
devotion with room for honest, loving anger
a vow of silence kept before the gods at dawn

games.q: dawn at the bower — tap the pairs.
p: red from a night without sleep

s: the poem quickly corrects Radha for being angry
it lets her anger stand. only later does her friend tell her she's held on long enough.
Vaishnava poetics treats mana as one of love's real moods
loving anger is named and honored, not hidden as a fault.
Radha welcomes Krishna in at dawn without a word
she sends him away: don't speak your deceiving words.

games.q: you're Radha. you waited all night. at dawn he turns up, red-eyed, with marks of somewhere else. what do you do?
o: let him in and say nothing.
tell him to go, and say exactly why.
leave the forest before he sees you.
games.why: she tells him to go: don't speak your deceiving words. the poem lets her say it all, and Krishna keeps seeking her anyway.

practice: Let the shoulders drop and bring to mind one disappointment you've been carrying quietly, with a person, with life, or with God, if God is part of your life.
Don't argue it away or make it bigger; just name it to yourself, plainly, the way Radha does, and notice that you're still here, still facing it.
If you pray, bring it into your prayer just as it is; if you don't, let it be said inside, and keep breathing.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti. Devotion. In the Gita Govinda it has room for mana, love's honest anger, which still keeps facing the beloved.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: mana, here the wounded pride of a lover. In Vaishnava poetry it is Radha's mood of loving anger.

carryVoice: Your line: bhakti has room for honest anger at God. Even her go-away kept her facing him. That's day nine hundred seventy-nine.

sources.ref: Gita Govinda, Radha's waiting in the bower and her dawn song (refrain 'yahi madhava yahi keshava ma vada kaitava vadam')
